title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation failure, but the AI system involved is not a deployed product gone wrong in the conventional sense. Instead, scammers used AI tools to fabricate a convincing fake news article, complete with a fictional interview between two real, named public figures, in order to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The failure is not inside a legitimate deployment but in the offensive use of AI-generated content to deceive consumers at scale. The fabrication was credible enough to circulate as apparent journalism, which is the core risk: AI generation lowered the cost and raised the quality of disinformation to the point where ordinary skepticism is insufficient to catch it.

The broader pattern ASIC describes is one of layered deception, fake articles feeding fake websites feeding fake investment platforms, each element reinforcing the others. The scale ASIC reports, tens of thousands of scams removed in a single year with percentage increases in the hundreds, suggests that no single point of human review is catching these before they reach victims. The point of failure is distribution, where fabricated content reaches social media feeds and search results before any verification occurs.

What is not established is who created the specific fake Kohler-Bullock article, whether any victims lost money to Boulder Sparhaven specifically, or what AI tools were used to produce the material.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fabricated article circulated online featuring a fake interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The fake story, which never actually occurred, depicted Bullock storming out over Kohler's questions. This incident exemplifies a growing category of scams using artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfakes of celebrities and politicians. ASIC reports that such schemes are becoming increasingly sophisticated and prevalent.

ASIC's latest research reveals that investment scams jumped significantly, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams surged 279 percent, while fake investment platforms rose 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tops the list of impersonated public figures, followed by other politicians and financial experts. Scammers create elaborate deception networks combining fake news articles, websites, and advertisements to lure victims. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers independently and remain skeptical of investment opportunities promoted by famous faces.
